utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. This is the north-west corner of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to note the -- first off, the dark matter in the corner and the darkened wood floor-boards when you first entered the room, and what was your first -- initial observations and your ultimate conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Well, my initial observations from when I first walked in the door, I thought I saw several patterns in the back corner, which later on were identified as human feces, which were some of the darkened spots in that soled plank area. Now, the area towards the bottom of the photo, I inspected that area, and it actually goes a little bit further down on one of the other photos. I inspected this area here because this was the darkest and blackest area. And from the initial photographs that I had reviewed before going to the scene, it appeared to be fire damage to me, so I was curious to examine it. Once I got to the examination of it, I did note that there was some burned pieces of wood in this area, but on the edge of it, on the -- one of the other photographs, I actually found that the first part, most of the blackening is done due to the mold and moisture content. On one of the pieces of the wood, I did actually snap it off and inspect it visually and felt it just to see if it had any fire damage. Now, in this particular photo, the centre -- I believe it's more over to the right just maybe -- on my screen, maybe an inch up. I did note that there was some burn patterns there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take it one step at a time. First of all, you indicated that you did physically snap off a piece of wood from the floor to conduct an examination of it. Could you tell us approximately where in reference to the room that procedure was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Actually, it was just on the edge of this photo. It's not depicted in this particular photo. It's approximately maybe one foot further down from that one large plank in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can enter this exhibit -- sorry, tender this picture as an exhibit into evidence as the next 1D number, and then if we can call up -- let's try 3617 to see if that's the area that Mr. Dimas is referencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this provide a better vantage point from what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No. The exhibit that has the best overall view, there's actually -- I believe it's like a little kettle or a pot, a metal pot of some sort on the right-hand side. It's a wider-angle view. It covers more of the flooring.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. If we can pull up Y020-3584, Your Honours. I think that's the one that I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when that photograph comes up, Mr. Dimas, does this appear to be the photograph that -- the view that you were referencing in your prior discussion and answer?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us what you visually observed at the scene when viewing this particular portion of the floor where the floor appears to be somewhat intact, and if you could with the assistance of the court assistants perhaps mark anything that you would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to that is of significance in terms of your conclusions and findings relative to the Pionirska Street location.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Okay. First, I'll point out the area that I actually broke off a piece of wood and tested it by manually, physically feeling it, examining it. It was basically in this area here. Somewhere in that area there, snapped off a piece. Would you like me to switch colours for the next portion or keep the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't we keep it the same for the time being, and we'll denote that the area where you snapped off the wood has been marked in a red circle towards the lower left-hand corner of the photograph, I would say closer to the middle than to the left corner.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Okay. The one area I did note that had some burning and charring was in this area here. In particular, we had some good charring on this piece of wood, and other pieces around this area. What I didn't note was during this investigation there was obvious signs that somebody has been in the structure, obviously. I don't know if they're camping out or what due to the human feces. You have actual remains of bones, consisting more like a chicken bone or animal bone right here and right here; so it wouldn't be impossible that that's where they're cooking their meat on. Again, it had the appearance that somebody's been living in here since the time of the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the drawings that you've made, if you could please put an A next to the area -- next to the circle that you drew where you broke off a piece of the wood flooring.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if you could mark with a B the area where you indicated that there was some charring and you said that persons were camping out.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And lastly, if you could mark with a C the locations where you stated that you found some type of chicken bones.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I want to ask you a question about this location. Using your knowledge and experience that you have as an investigator of fires, do you believe that any fire that occurred in the area for cooking -- that you indicated for cooking food based upon the other evidence that's at this site would have fully enveloped the room that is in question?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No. The amount of damage you see is limit to this one area right here. You can see the unburned portion of the wood along the edge. When you have a fire that grows to intensity to consume a room, it's called flash-over. You need to get a temperature that reaches an excess of 1200 degrees Fahrenheit, and you'd have to have the fuel load or material to burn to reach that type of temperature, and what's here is just not enough to reach those temperatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation to catch up with us. And now with respect to the floor-boards, were there also portions of the floor-board that were -- I believe in our discussions, you'd described them to me as pristine condition.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. In regards to the floor, we can see some of them. In addition, throughout the whole room we actually found another piece that was under one of the windows in question that was unaffected by fire or flame of any type.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, what does the existence of this pristine-condition wood do for any hypotheses or any conclusions that you draw as to whether, in fact, this room was subjected to a fully enveloped fire that affected all the -- that would have affected all the interior of the room?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: In a fully evolved structure fire, it affects everything one way or another. It doesn't have to be burning, charring, but you're going to have sooting, some type of staining, especially with wood. Wood is porous and it absorbs things of that nature. Basically, patterns can be transferred three ways: You have consumption, that's when it would eat the item up, such as the charring you see on wood. It's been eaten up by the fire; you have the deposition or the depositing of items such as soot; and the other one is just by heat itself, and what we're talking there is, say, a plastic item too close to a camp-fire or you heat your straw up too much. It tends to melt, and we don't see anything like that in this fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, just to clarify, you say with respect to this fire that we've been talking about, this camp-fire, my question was with respect to the room as a whole. Do you see any evidence to a fully developed -- fully evolved fire having been in this room that would encountered all the interior in?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke myself I used the camp-fire just as a reference to what you'd see when you got too close to -- a plastic item to a heat. As far as -- excuse me, Your Honours. What I described earlier was, I meant it for in a fully evolved structure fire. The camp-fire reference was to strictly to try to make it so more people would understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is there anything else with this particular picture that we have on the e-court right now that you could -- that assists you in assisting us understand your conclusions, or shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: The only other item in relation to this is whenever I do find any type of burn pattern, I don't only just look at the floor. I look at what's in close proximity or what's above it because we all know a fire goes up and out, so I did look at the ceiling level of this, and I didn't find any damage consistent with the fire being of great intensity underneath it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's one of the areas I was going to ask you about. Now, when you say you looked at the ceiling, did you note -- what was the condition in the room in terms of the moisture? Was there any signs of active seepage into the room either through the walls or through the ceiling as you observed them?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. There was moisture throughout. First off, the floor was very damp and moist. The ceiling was actually in act of dripping of water. We did note -- I forget which ones come from the ceiling, stalagtites or stalagmites, but the water growth coming off the ceiling, and there was active dripping coming from the ceiling in multiple areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this. There's been some suggestion that wood that has been charred as a result of fire, that water and environmental aspects can remove -- basically remove or wash off the evidence of fire damage. What effect does the presence of water have on wood that has been subjected to a fire and has been charred and/or subjected to alligatoring? What effect does water have on that type of wood, generally speaking, based upon your experience?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Actually, with wood -- with anybody who's every dealt with any type of wood, any time you introduce moisture, the moisture actually helps preserve it because it doesn't dry out. So whatever condition it's in by the time it gets moisture, that's how it would stay. So actually, it would help preserve the fire damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So had there been hypothetically a fully evolved fire confined in this area, the basement room, would you expect to have found evidence -- more extensive evidence of it than you saw of the condition of these floor-boards by the camp-fire area and the other areas that you have indicated?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. That was one reason why I examined the edge of where I marked A at. Since that was the leading edge of it, I want to see what type of damage that was, and again, that was a smooth, slick area to the touch; whereas the noted alligatoring was in the centre. It wasn't a progression either way. It was isolate to where B is labelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And had there been a fully evolved fire in this room, in your opinion would there have been the possibility for the mold to cover up the evidence of that fire?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, there wouldn't be that much because there's a lot of areas in there that are very limited on the moisture. Like I said, there's a great deal, but the moisture doesn't encompass the whole room. What I should probably note out is when we look at fire patterns, patterns give us two indicators. They show us the movement or direction of travel as well as the intensity of a fire, and that's why we're looking for patterns. They tell us which way it's going, and it leads us back to wherever the fire started. And again, the intensity, if it was a heavy fire, a weak fire, again, in a large-scale fire you'd see a lot of heavy damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can save the photograph as marked and tender it as the next available 1D exhibit, I'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And if we could in the meantime pull up 1D22-0603.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, sir, is it accurate that you found one other location that you singled out or pointed out as a potential small-scale fire in the basement room at the Pionirska residence?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Directly as you walk into the door on the left-hand side behind the door, again, the door opens inwards, so it's behind there between the door and the first window, I did find some remains of charred wood in that area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could have the second page of in document. I apologise. I think the second page has the portion that Mr. Dimas is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, I believe it's going to be photograph number 7 on the second page. Once it comes up, if you could take a look at that and tell us whether that is the locale that you're making reference to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That's not it either. I guess it's the next page, then. I apologise. Or 10. That's it, 10. Sorry. Too slow. If we could back up to the next -- previous page, and it's photograph number 10. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, if you could tell us if that is the -- if that is the location in question where you located evidence of a smaller-scale fire.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct, in the corner there. I found some charred wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And given the empirical evidence that you located, that is to say the charred wood that you located, was it in your opinion -- in your opinion, was that evidence for one to conclude that a large, fully enveloped fire occurred in this room?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, there was not. Again, all I did was I noted that there was charred remains right there. It goes back to doing a complete investigation and doing the totality of all the evidence. It was just one more item for me to note. Again, when I review all the evidence found on-scene, that's when I come to my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this particular document has been tendered during the testimony of Mr. McCoy, and I just recall that Your Honours are reserving ruling on this, so I will not tender this again. I'll just wait for the ruling in due course on that, and I'd like to move on to some more pictures as to the interior of the Pionirska location, and if we could call up Y020-3590.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, are you able to place yourself back in the room and describe for us where this window is located and where the -- where that corner that is depicted in the room is located? Is that -- where is that?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: This is the same area as the previous one. It's directly inside the room on the left-hand side as you walk through the door. That's the very first window, and the little fire debris that I noted was in that corner there, just basically from the corner to the edge of that wood beam.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there appears to be some dark discolouration of the wall visible in this photograph. Did you ascertain what that was, or did you draw any conclusions as to what that was?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was examined, and again, we found that there was a lot of moisture content in this area, a lot of mold. The pattern underneath the window that almost looks like a V, that is actually just moisture, so we didn't find any evidence of fire patterns in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you see to the left of the window there appears to be some sort of demarcation in the wall or line in the wall that appears to run from the top and goes underneath the window, actually. Did you visually observe that, and did you reach any conclusions as to what that was?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Are you describing the line on the left-hand side or the wood beam underneath? I'm sorry. I'm not sure what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify. I see some sort of a line to the left of the window but before the corner that appears to run down from somewhere up on top towards the area underneath the window and then curves towards the window. It looks like a black line in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. We took a look at that specifically because at the very top there's, like, a circular or square-type image on top of that line. Let me see if I have you correct. You're talking about this line here? That -- and then this up here, I first noted the opening in the top. It appeared initially as being burned. We actually -- actually looked up into it, and we determined it to be more of a junction box. We actually found that the straight line there and one of the lines coming over here were actually electrical wires which were actually plastered into the wall itself, so the darkness, it's just due to being a black hole that's been filled with water mold, what have you, but that's actually an electrical junction box.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can have the picture as marked tendered as the next available 1D exhibit number, and then hopefully I can call up a clearer photograph of that area: Y020- -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar, and I apologise for preempting you. If I can have Y020-3579 and perhaps alongside it, Y020-3578.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, while we wait for those, I hope those will be better photographs of the area that you've described so as to permit you to -- no. I apologise. That's the wrong number. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Madam Registrar. Can I have Y020-3633 and alongside it, Y020-3634. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do these provide a better vantage point of that which you were describing to the upper left of the window?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. The square in the centre, again, if you just look at a photo, it looks to be almost like a wood item inside, when actually it's just an opening, and there's nothing inside of it. However, these lines here and here were actually to identify those as wires coming into that box.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can have this screenshot saved with the markings attached and admitted as the next 1D exhibit number. I'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've been working our way from the floor upwards systematically. I'd like to ask you a few questions now about the ceiling, and with respect to the ceiling, could you describe for us what spalling is, and what are the potential causes of spalling.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Spalling is a phenomenon that occurs in mortar, concrete, and brick; and basically, it's the expansion of the water molecules within those -- in those forms, and it can be caused either by heat or by severe cold. And what happens is just causes expansion and contraction of the water molecules, which makes the edges, basically, for lack of a better word, pop and bust outward, and that's what spalling is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that because of the various causes or various potential causes for spalling that, therefore, you look at other factors in addition to spalling before reaching any final conclusion as to whether certain damage is based upon exposure to heat, flame, or smoke or something else?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. In previous years, spalling used to be held as a pure indication that ignitable liquid had been used. Then over the course of the years, it was learned that it was more than just rapid heat. That's when it was determined that it was due to the water molecules and since that time is no longer one set indicator that any kind of an accelerant or excessive heat was utilised. So in that matter, that's why we can only use it as what we see. It's just another indicator that something occurred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So at the time that you visited the Pionirska site in January 2009, what was the -- what was the overall totality of the condition of the ceiling? Was it in good shape, bad shape? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: It was in very poor shape due to the extreme water and moisture that were seeping in. There was a lot of parts that were falling down. I mentioned the little calcium or water stalagtites off the ceiling dripping down, so there were areas that had actually collapsed downward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now with respect to the ceiling, do you recall locating and examining a hole in the ceiling that led up to the next level in the Pionirska structure?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. When you walk in just off to the right-hand side, approximately I'd say four feet into the building, there is an opening going up to the second floor. I was unable to determine what it was used for. There was no type of pipe-work inside of it. It was just maybe a three-inch-diameter hole going up to the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, assuming for the moment in a hypothetical that a fully evolved fire took place in the basement room and enveloped that room, what would the existence of that circular opening in the ceiling mean with respect to the fire and to the by-products of a fire?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Fire is much like water. It seeks the path of least resistance to travel, so that's why we'll look at any type of opening or penetration within a structure. That's why we look at the doors and windows. In this case, this one was of great importance considering it's going upward, and I stated earlier, fires as we all know travel up and out. So if there was a fire inside this room, it would have let upstairs to the next room, and upon examining that opening, found no evidence or no trace of any soot or by-products of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you -- let's ask you this question first. Do you consider it plausible for there to have been a fire that would have not left such residue and markings in the interior of this hole in the ceiling, and perhaps -- perhaps to assist while you're answering that question, if we can call up Y020-3361.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No. Again, any type of fire that would be generally near it or next to it, as we all know, if have you a fireplace it would have that chimney effect. The smoke would go up and rise into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, unfortunately, in this photograph we don't have a measuring tool or a ruler there to determine the diameter. You, I believe, indicated it was 3 inches?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Approximately 3 inches, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the rough interior that we see here, what -- what would that rough interior mean in regards to any residue or any soot or any smoke billowing through this hole from a fire in the basement room up to the next level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It occurs to me that this is essentially a repeat of what Mr. McCoy has testified to. The report has been tendered. I'm not sure that I see the point of having two people testify to exactly the same thing when both reports are now in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have been considering the same, Mr. Ivetic. What's the point of this evidence which seems to be a replication of earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have evidence that is still not accepted by the Office of the Prosecutor which is still being objected to by the Office of the Prosecutor. We have two individuals of varying experience and varying qualifications who examined the Pionirska location on behalf of the Defence. We have Mr. Dimas here who as we see in his CV and the limited review of his experience is the one who does quality control of the work of other fire/arson investigators, and he himself has had similar experience in regards to this; and it goes towards corroboration of the assertions that the Defence has made, and it goes to explaining the portions of his report why he, in particular, believes this photograph and what it shows is significant to his conclusion. And again, it's something that the Defence cannot anticipate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the chimney? Just for another two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just please conclude the examination-in-chief. Go ahead, Judge Van den Wyngaert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I have a question. It seems that the two experts visited the place at the same time together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Why didn't you have them draft one report signed by the both of them? What's the purpose of the duplication because we are hearing exactly the same from a different person in this same case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the main things that the fire investigators explained to me was peer review is essential. This is a cold case, obviously, so with the limitations imposed, they wanted two sets of eyes. Mr. Dimas is the lead investigator, and I think the Prosecution used the junior status of Mr. McCoy to their theory of the case, but the reality is the meat and bones of the investigation was performed by Mr. Dimas, who is the lead and senior investigator. Mr. McCoy was meant to carry the camera and of course has similar qualifications but was not in the role of lead investigator on this mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two or three more questions, then. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would point out that's what's being pointed out that what is being presented now is a lead investigator and junior investigator was presented to the Court earlier today and last week as two qualified experts in fire -- identification of fire causes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can ask the witness to explain that. That was one of the areas I was going to go into in his prior experience that I had to short-circuit, so if that's something that Your Honours are interested in, the gentleman's here. He can explain the standard operation procedure is in his employment and his line of work and what the significance found to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just ask your two more questions and let's move on to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have also Bikavac, which will be about five or six questions as to the Bikavac site, the second site that was sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. I think I had a question pending. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to repeat the question that I had asked prior to this exchange, and it was: Given the rough surface that we see in this interior leading up to this hole in the second level, what does that lead you to conclude or expect as to any smoke or fire markers, i.e. residue of soot? What effect does this un-smooth surface have on the collection of any of those trace matters?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Well, with it being uneven, porous, you'd still find, again, evidence of some type of sooting or collection of fire up in there, mainly sooting and ash, maybe, if there had been a fire there because ash tends to float, as well, and there is no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any measurement or approximation as to the distance between the beginning of this whole in the ceiling and its termination point, that is to say how deep or how long is this going upwards?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: It would be just whatever the thickness the slab was because it ends on the floor of the second storey or the ground floor, so it's only from the basement ceiling to the floor of the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could -- if we could just to be safe tender this as an exhibit, Your Honours; I note that this exhibit was used with Mr. McCoy, but my notes indicate that the one that he viewed, he marked up, so I'd like to have a clean copy as well. One moment. Yeah, I think it's illustrative to have a clean copy tendered. The one that was previously tendered by Mr. McCoy has markings on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Dimas, I'd like to move to the last area that we had, will be brief as I know your investigations of that site were brief. We also went to the Bikavac location. Is that accurate, and what can you tell us about your trained observations as to the Bikavac site? Is there anything that you can assist us as to that?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: The scene exam was very limited since there was no structure left. Again, there I observed what appeared to be the remains of the foundation, some footings or footers that were out of concrete. I dug into a couple areas within the dirt, again, looking for fire debris or ash. I made note of areas where I found some black residue. That was pretty much the extent of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the black residue, what, if any, conclusions or observations did you draw as to that?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: It was determined to be a tar substance. When I noted the nearby other buildings, it appears that they use it as a sealer within their buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the Bikavac site itself, could you describe for us as one of the few persons in this courtroom who's actually been to the location physically, how difficult was it to get there, and what was the surrounding terrain like and the location of the houses like around the site where the Bikavac location was situated?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: We had a slight difficulty. Going -- the main road going up to it was uphill. One of the vehicles had difficulty with its clutch. Once we got onto the side street leading up to the house, that was very muddy and narrow. Both roads were very narrow, so even in the small car we had difficulty reaching the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the neighboring houses, the neighboring houses to the empty lot where the Bikavac site was located? What can you say about the distances between or how close they were to that site?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: The edges of the foundation after we identified edge to edge was very close in proximity to two homes. On one side, there's a house that's approximately three storeys again. It was probably within three feet of that structure, and then on the other side that side was maybe 6 feet away, so very close proximity, so that's always a concern especially in a fully evolved structure fire because fire can radiate or be spread to other buildings nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. One moment. Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, I believe the photographs of the -- that had been selected by the experts for inclusion in their report is the -- has been tendered through Mr. McCoy, and we're just waiting the ultimate determination of the Trial Chamber, so I do not need to tender those photographs a second time, I don't believe. And with that, I have no further questions on direct examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dimas. My name is Dermot Groome, and I'm going to ask you some questions. The first question I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: A moment. I apologise, Mr. Groome. We got via e-mail during the direct examination of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this discussion not be in front of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this weekend the Prosecution went down to look at the site again and has some evidence I'd like to show Mr. Dimas. I'd ask that Mr. Alarid not be coaching through his objections Mr. Dimas about what it is that Mr. Alarid now knows we intend to show Mr. Dimas during this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I don't know. We haven't been produced this evidence. It is Rule 68 and -- whatever the rule is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us deal with it when Mr. Groome gets to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Excuse me? I apologise, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're anticipating what Mr. Groome will produce in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's video and photographs, apparently, and evidence collected at the site that he's saying was part of his mission on this particular weekend. I think we should have an opportunity to been presented this evidence if it's going to be tendered in open court, and we should be tender this evidence before he questions the witness on it. And so under those circumstances, Your Honour, I think it's just common courtesy in terms of producing evidence that if they had it, and if it was producible this morning, it should have been tendered to us this morning. The fact that it's not tendered to us until during the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, is that going to be your first business, first part of business in your cross-examination to tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, it will not be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. When you come to it, then we'll deal wilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct in stating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Defence spent two hours, and I'm expecting you will use just about the same time, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct in saying that you and Mr. McCoy both discussed your conclusions in this case and are in agreement in all material ways about your conclusions about your examination at Pionirska Street; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That's not necessarily true. As part of peer review, what we do --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, as you can tell, I'm very limited in the time I have. What finding do you disagree with Mr. McCoy?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Well, the findings or evidence, like, for example, I'm not sure what Mr. McCoy fully testified to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about his report? Let's just look at the two reports. Are you in full agreement with everything he said in his report?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I actually did not read his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So how does peer review occur if you don't read his report? Do you simply just discuss what are your observations?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes. We bounce off the -- what we're visually seeing on-site. Again, I was the lead investigator on the scene, so I'm bouncing of what I'm seeing and to see if somebody else sees something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You were shown a video in your direct examination taken in 2001. You've seen the entire video; have you not?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And throughout that video, there are many soldiers with masks on and heavy weapons; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would ill be correct in saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just a problem in translation in B/C/S. Both speakers have been speaking quite fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise to the translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are speaking very fast. Please slow down and observe the pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be reasonable for anyone looking at that video-tape to conclude that security was of paramount concern during the time that video was taken; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you do not know as you sit here whether there was possible concern for possible mines inside that building or in the area; do you?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, I don't dispute that. What I stated was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I finish my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I stated earlier was if there was such great concern, they could have at least held the video into the window. If they did have an armed guard right there who peered in. Why not document it with the camera it self?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It may be that the decision about what soldiers can do and what civilian photographers can do might be different, but there's really no need for us to dwell on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that 1D169 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this picture that's coming up now is the picture of the charred material - it seems everyone agrees it's charred - in the portico. Now, correct, this is to the right of the door in the portico; correct.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So standing looking at the front door of the room, it would be to your right still under the portico?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, sir. You go to the right of the doorway, it's actually on the left-hand corner of that portico.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it's to the right of the doorway?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, to the right of the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask -- Mr. Ivetic introduced 1D184. It's a video. I'm going ask that you show a still of this. I'm going to ask that it be placed on the ELMO. So if that could be placed on the overhead projector to your right, we'll all be able to see, and if we could zoom out a little bit. Now, sir, you've mentioned this -- I think you've referred to it as a shed. It looks like a boarded-up area to the right of the door; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, it has the appearance of some type of structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the burnt that material that we see on 1D169 is not visible from this standpoint, is it?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it is impossible to know that this video taken nine years after the fire, whether or not the material on the wall there is burnt or isn't burnt; is that not correct.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Can you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's impossible from this video to tell whether or not the burnt material in 1D169, whether it's sitting up there in 2001 burnt or it's un-burnt. It's impossible for you to tell that, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That's correct. You can't tell either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you seem to suggest in your evidence that the fire damage or whatever we see in the portico must be the result of a fire that involved this shed because we no longer see this shed material; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Not necessarily the shed, but there is a fire within where that shed existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you believe that this shed material burnt down in the same fire that we see the charred material from 1D169?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I couldn't say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So it's quite possible that this shed material was simply taken down and there was never a fire involved in its removal; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Because you've testified that there's no fire damage on the door. If this shed structure were to be destroyed by fire, you would expect to see some fire damage on the door so close by; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I draw your attention to the -- above the door. Do you see that very black area above the door? Could I ask you to circle that so that we know that we're talking about the same -- the same section.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I can ask while we're doing this, if we could prepare to work with P270. It's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that the area you're discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, except it looks like it extends all the way to the left.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Oh, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you can't say that this is not smoke damage, can you?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how can you -- are you able to say that that's not smoke damage?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Because I was physically at the site and examined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, are you able to say that this isn't -- this is not charred material?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this look the same as the way you saw it at the site?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No. Actually, there's less of it now because of the time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it possible this is what we're looking at is the same charred material you found to the right but now in your January visit it's now missing?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not possible?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we could take a look at P270.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, on your report, which is now 1D183, you refer to a beam, and earlier in your direct testimony at transcript 49, you refer to a beam as a pristine piece of wood. I want to be sure that we're talking about the same piece of wood, okay? Okay, it should be up on the screen in front of you. Do you see the piece of wood circled at the bottom that's circled in blue?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the piece of wood that you describe as a beam that is pristine?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McCoy has testified similarly. Is it at all possible that this could be a piece of furring strip used as a means of attaching a piece of finished wall surface to the wall?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I examined it to see if anything might be attached to it, and I did find a couple of nail holes or nails actually in it, but in conjunction to everything else I eliminated anything been attach to it. Simply, it was a clean piece of wood with two nails in it. Again, I do the totality of all of my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McCoy described it as a piece of wood, a beam embedded in the concrete. Is that your recollection of the piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you come to the conclusion that it was actually embedded in the concrete wall?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Because the concrete is flush with the edges of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to ask that you be shown two pictures at the same time on the screen. The first is Y020-3396, and the second is Y020-3359. If they could be placed side by side on the screen. Okay. Now, what I'm interested in -- let's look at the picture on your left, 3396. See that black line up there?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Running horizontally. Can I ask you to circle it so that, again, we're both sure that we're talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall where in the room that was?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That was on the -- that'd be the east wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I've put the other picture there, hopefully to assist you. This is the area to the left of the door. We can see the door jamb in the right-hand side of the frame. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, so I stand corrected. That's actually the south wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So am I correct in saying that the black line that we see here that you've circled is to the left of the door at the upper portion of the wall?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you examine this area?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I looked at the wall. I don't specifically remember doing this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you find any evidence of charring on this wall?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you examine the black material that's embedded in the concrete?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I take it, then, you didn't take a sample of it either?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that we tender the -- either the entire screenshot or the -- well, actually, the entire screenshot, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P303, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the ceiling, on page 2 of your report you say: "Areas of concern ..." for windows walls and ceiling, and under item 2(A), you state: "Areas show no V-patterns, sooting, or spalling associated with normal fire patterns." Is it your evidence that the ceiling showed no signs of spalling?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. I ruled it out based on the deterioration of the ceiling area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I please ask that we look at on e-court Y020-3622.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe where this is in the room?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That's actually on the east wall, towards the north edge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For those of us who might prefer a reference point from the door, if someone were to stand in the door's threshold looking into the room, which wall would it be on?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That would be on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Same wall that the flue or the -- what you describe, I think, as a pipe chase is on?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Actually, I did not use the term "pipe chase." I just said an opening, but yes, it's the same wall, and it's approximately 5 feet further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. What are your observations and conclusions about the blackened material that we see in those pockets in the wall to the right of the clay tile?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Actually, what I found was the one in the centre specifically, it had a chunk of charred wood embedded in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you found a piece of charred wood embedded in the wall. That didn't make its way into your report, did it?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, sir, it did not. Again, what I took what I found and I noted it down, and again, it's the totality of everything. I'm not going to list if I find one little speck in one corner of each area. I'm going to take my findings altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions. Now --

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's me that's asking the questions, sir. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: You asked me a question. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Groome. Let him finish. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I did do is normally when I find a chunk of wood coming out of a room, I try to determine if there's any correlation to it like a rafter going from one end of the wall to another, and I did not. So I did noted down that I find a chunk of wood in this wall. I was able to physically pull it out. It was not stuck in there. It was just a piece of wood in the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said you noted it down. Where did you note it down.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: In my notes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I please have a copy of those notes I'm entitled to?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Actually, it's our policy that we destroy all our notes after we write a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the notes have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, where you found this charred wood was rather close to the ceiling of this room; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Actually, it's about a foot away approximately. From floor to ceiling, it's about seven feet high.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that you did not think it was significant to mention in your report or your direct evidence here today that you found a piece of charred wood about 7 feet off the floor?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No because I couldn't determine how it got there. There was charred wood on the floor, in the flooring that was left; so it could have been somebody took the piece of wood, jammed it up there for what reason; I have no idea. Again, it's a piece of burned wood in the wall by itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is this tile where Mr. O'Donnell recovered what he believed to be a fragment of a grenade?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No. Actually, that would be further to the left-hand of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, on page 2 of your report, again, you list areas of concern for windows, walls, and ceilings; again, that there's no sooting or V-patterns. Did you do a careful examination of the exterior window of the basement room?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you have find anything that could be considered smoke damage?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to the door. On page 2 of your report again, you say: "Door and door jamb examined and showed no charring, sooting, or any type of fire damage. Door also opened into the structure. Area between the door jamb and block wall was examined for sooting or venting patterns through penetrations and showed ..." I believe you mean no fire patterns. You have two fire patterns. Did you mean no fire patterns?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I meant no fire patterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's time for the break. We'll resume at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that the witness be instructed not to discuss his testimony with anybody during the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, are you not to discuss your testimony with anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alarid, the Chamber has been trying to find additional court hours. It's possible that we may be able to sit tomorrow morning, and I will let you know. Mr. Groome, that presents a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not that, Your Honour, but there's a related matter I'd like to address in terms of scheduling very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm let you know at the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I also wanted to say to you, Mr. Alarid, you gave us an overview of your witnesses for the week, and if we are able to sit morning and afternoon on some of the days for the rest of the week, then we might reach Mr. Groome's rebuttal witnesses because we're going to give a decision on that tomorrow. So Mr. Groome should stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour. It's hard, but if I could address one scheduling matter with the Chamber. At the end of last week, Mr. Alarid advised us that the order of witnesses this week would be Mr. Dimas, then Mr. Jenkins, and then Dr. Hough. Today when court started, he said that they'd be shifting around Hough and Jenkins. I now see that the Chamber has given a ruling where Prosecution will have access -- I've only read the disposition. I haven't read the entire ruling, but I think that I've concluded that the Chamber is going to grant us access to some of this material. It's -- or maybe I'm wrong. Are we not getting the audio-tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No. We didn't rely on the audio tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I haven't gotten a chance to read --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll have to check on that. I can't remember off-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm asking is that Mr. Alarid be instructed to produce the witnesses in the order that they were noticed to us last week. Ms. Sartorio is doing Dr. Hough. There may be some additional material that the Prosecution is getting. We would ask that the noticed order be maintained. It was switched around last week and it caused me to lose a night's sleep. I would ask that we maintain the order as it's given to us on the Friday before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. Alarid. Why are you switching it around?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, because we're two people and we're trying to prepare -- Your Honour, if you give this Prosecution consideration for losing a night's sleep when they have nine attorneys to rotate through witnesses -- well, that's crazy. We have to do the best we can with the 24 hours, man hours we have on a particular day between two human beings, and that's all we have. And the fact that they get granted everything and we get granted nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That is how I feel. That is how I feel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no basis for that comment whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That is -- I think the record is replete --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us adjourn, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quickly, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, briefly it goes to the matter at hand, which is the Prosecution has just shown me several bags containing apparent material from the location known as Pionirska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's -- why don't you wait until they put it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- well, Your Honour, here's the problem: No foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that the Prosecution chose to present a case with no expert forensic examination of the properties before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to introduce that in your cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, wait until that time. Why are you preempting it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I do not wish to hear you. Sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It asks you to assume facts not in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, continue the cross-examination. Wait your turn. Don't waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Dimas, before I resume my questions about the door, I wanted to ask you, given that you were one of the people that recently drafted the new standard operating guidelines, what is the underlying rationale why fire investigators of the Albuquerque Fire Department are instructed to destroy the notes that they take at a fire scene after they've drafted their report? What's the rationale, please?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Just that there's no need for them after you've written your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But haven't we just demonstrated that it's of critical need because here's this piece of charred wood in the wall that was in your notes but not in the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me turn to your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is correct? You have put two propositions to you, and you have said "that is correct." Are you agreeing with him that what has been demonstrated is that -- would you repeat the question, Mr. Groome, because I'm not sure the witness understood it when he said that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you, sir, is that you've admitted that you have -- you noticed something in the charred wood in the wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You say that you noted your observations about charred wood in the wall in your notes, but you never put that in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what I'm saying to you now is, you have just testified that the reason that the notes are destroyed is because there is no need for them once you've drafted the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There's no need for your notes after you've drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I guess what I'm suggesting to you is that you have just demonstrated that there is a need because there's a very important inconsistency between the notes that you took at the scene and the report that has now been tendered as evidence in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: No, there's not an inconsistency. It's just again it's just a totality of all your evidence that you found. You don't have to include everything as I stated earlier. If I noted that there's one piece of ash in the centre of the room and I had made note of that, I wouldn't include that in my report either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the reason you did not record in the report your discovery of charred wood near the ceiling of the centre of the room was because you did not deem it important for your report?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. In addition, we also had it as photographic evidence that we could discuss it in -- in putting the two together and discussing it, that's when you can actually point out what you were seeing as we did here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I did not make note in the report, but I can demonstrate it on the photographic evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything else about your observations when you examined the scene that did not make it into your report? So even if you think it's insignificant, I'm asking you to list for me any other observations you made at the scene which you did not include in your report.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I don't believe that I listed that the patterns above on the second floor where there is actual wood that shows fire damage. There's fire patterns up there. I didn't include that many my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you did have that in your notes?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else in your notes that did not make it into your report? Let's -- to save time, if we could focus on the basement room and the portico. Is there any other observations you made about either of those two locations, in the basement, that you noted in your notes but you deemed that it wasn't important enough to put into your report?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I didn't list, as well, the pit marks that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: -- Mr. O'Donnell was investigating. I didn't feel that was necessary for my report. Again, we did photograph it, and if it came up, I could explain and describe what I'd seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So other than that, is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you draw the conclusion that the door that's presently there is the original door?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I didn't determine it either way. What I did was I examined it for burn patterns, as I put in my report, the door itself, the door jamb. I tried to see which way it opened, which way it swung. I did have concerns as to the hinge marks and the locking area being incorrect. That was another thing I did not note in my report, but I did observe it, and it was photographed, and I explained it here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you put that in your notes?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it seems that you're saying now that you really don't know or you can't say with any certainty that the door was the same door that was there the night of the fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I never stated that, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All you can state is that what you observed, you made certain observations about black mold and no presence of any kind of fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you accept the possibility that the door may have been changed?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, the door may have changed, and that is one reason why I examined the gaps between the door jamb and the concrete that it would have been attached to to see if there was any damage in between because had they removed the door, there still should have been some sort of damage in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. McCoy drew the conclusion that it was the original door. Is that a conclusion that the two of you discussed?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I never discussed that with him. Again, it was my understanding coming out here I was the lead investigator and had been chosen so by Your Honours. Mr. McCoy was supposed to be down here to be my photographer and to be a person I could ask questions to to see what he was seeing, but it was my determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we call up Defence Exhibit 1D174.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It'll take a few minutes to call that up. While it's being called up, in paragraph 3 of the first page of your report which is now in evidence as 1D183, you state: "I performed a systematic approach beginning with the exterior of the structure trying to identified any type of burn patterns or fire indicators." Now it seems in the evidence that you've given in the last few minutes and in direct examination that you did do an overview of the entire structure, not simply the basement; correct.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you an exhibit that was used with your colleague Mr. McCoy. It is 1D174. It is a picture of the upper floor of the house. The floor has very obviously burned away. Mr. McCoy testified that he saw smoke damage here. In fact, let me read to you what he testified to at transcript page 5824: "There is smoke damage, smoke discolouration in a V-pattern above that timber." And this corresponds to the marks that he made. "It's darker coloured areas of the tile. Arson investigators, we're trained to read patterns. That's what leads us to the origin." Has Mr. McCoy correctly outlined the area in which smoke damage is apparent to the trained arson investigator?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: First off, let's correct the terminology. It's fire investigator. You have to investigate the fire before you make the determination of it being an arson or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I stand corrected. So fire investigator, with that correction.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: He does make a lot of good points, or he has noted a lot of items here. He did miss a few other patterns here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we go on to additional smoke damage, if we can focus on what he indicates as a V-pattern of smoke damage coming up from that timber. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be given a red pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It seems that you see additional smoke damage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If we can change the pen to red.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you could show us the smoke damage that Mr. McCoy missed.

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: I'd say that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'd ask that that be -- I would tender that exhibit under a new number, and if we could leave it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dimas, the evidence provided by Mr. McCoy and yourself raises a very significant issue in the trial. You see seven people escape that fire; six of them gave sworn evidence before this Chamber. The seventh died after the fire, but his son recounted what happened that night. All seven are resolute in their account that over 65 women, children, and elderly burnt to death in that room, never seen after the night of the fire. The evidence of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you saying that's a misstatement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's been no testimony that -- or foundation laid that the fire that enveloped the upper levels of this house was related to the alleged incident that these witnesses testified to, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would add, Your Honour, just with regards to 65 women, children, and elderly, the witnesses of those referenced by Mr. Groome vary greatly on whom they identified as being part of the group, and that is one of our issues with regards to proper victims or alleged victims being named in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you want me to respond to that, Your Honour, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking him to focus on the basement room, although there has been testimony that not only with the upper floors but the two Memic houses were burned that night, but I'm just asking the witness about the bottom floor. With respect to the exact number of witnesses, I'll leave that to the Chamber. I thought I was being fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But let me just reword it, sir. A substantial, substantial number of women, children, and elderly, seven people say died in the room where you say no fire occurred. Now, it's just simply irreconcilable; either those witnesses are deceiving this Chamber or you and Mr. McCoy are. Do you fully appreciate the predicament that your evidence now places us in?

utterances.speaker: BENJAMIN DIMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I utilised some of the witness statements to add into what I was finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I sat here Friday when Mr. McCoy was telling us that there was apparent smoke damage on these walls, and I could not see none, and I still could not see any. And I thought I had to make a choice between believing Mr. McCoy and now believing you and believing my own eyes. So I went down over the weekend with some investigators. I want to show you some of the material that we brought back and some of what we saw when we went down there. I'm going to ask that you look at two video-clips, and I'm going ask that we use the Sanction system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this is the point, Your Honour. We've not been provided this in advance, and I believe that the Prosecution had the opportunity to provide this evidence this morning. We had a late day. There's no excuse for it not being provided in advance of the testimony. And what I'm objecting to, Your Honour, is in basic principle is we have an instance where a homicide case, the Prosecution has chosen to present its forensic examinations in rebuttal? In what jurisdiction can that be proper where no forensic exam is done and they're only doing it in response to us taking trained people down there? At the very least, Your Honour, the witness should have had an opportunity to review these photographs this morning. Concurrent to that, Your Honour, no foundation and proper foundation has been laid on this, and this violates the rules of disclosure. Thank you. And we still don't have them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you mean you still don't have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: They have not been produced to us. We have received no disks or the usual methods of giving us our copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have still not received them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No. What he's going to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's let him deal with that point first. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They're all in e-court. Your Honour will recall the ruling at the pre-trial conference. Upon cross-examination, the party is to notify the other party about what exhibits it seeks to use. I walked in this morning with these exhibits. They were -- we went down over the weekend. I would note that exhibits used with this witness were disclosed to me this morning, although also on the same pre-trial conference. We were required to disclose those to each other 48 hours in advance, so I am several days late on that. If I could finish my remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That was your exhibit we used, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the providence of where the exhibit came from is not the issue. The other party is to be notified 48 hours in advance of when before an exhibit is used with a witness. These were recently collected. I've complied with the Chamber's pre-trial conference ruling. I've made them available during the break for Mr. Alarid. They're all put out on the table here. He walked over, took a cursory look, and walked back to his desk. He had a full opportunity throughout the entire break to look at the exhibits here. They've been out since the beginning of the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me consult the Trial Chamber's order on this as to when notice to be given by the cross-examining party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we assumed that we'd also be provided -- notice is one thing, but we were never provided the actual materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And they are not in e-court and the e-mail that we received says we don't have reference numbers for these videos materials, so, therefore, Your Honours, they have never been tendered to us in any format whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So they are in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They are not in e-court. We have not been provided any reference numbers for them. We have not been provided copies of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you told me they are in e-court. They say they are not in e-court. What's the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. They're in Sanction. It's a different system. So I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sanction is an OTP-only system not available to either the Defence or the Registry, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is what we're going to do. We have 40 minutes until the end of the session. We are going to adjourn now. We're going to resume in the morning, and the Defence will be given the opportunity to look at these -- is it tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't believe the same right extends to the witness, so I would ask that the witness again because he's in the middle of his testimony not have communication with anyone overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, we would ask to be able to provide these to the witness. I mean, it's not -- the Prosecution's already asked Mr. McCoy to look at things overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can look at them but not the witness, he will show the witness them in court. That's a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: He's an expert, Your Honour. He is not of the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
